The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has launched, and it's glorious. But the real challenge isn't saving Hyrule as Link; it's finding a restock of the Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition Nintendo Switch 2 console.
Restocks are rolling out — Target and Nintendo recently dropped fresh chances to grab the hard-to-find console — and with Nintendo promising more stock is on the way, I'm bringing you the latest stock updates.
As of now, there is no Zelda Switch 2 restock available . However, multiple retailers are prioritizing in-store restocks (Best Buy, Walmart, GameStop), so if you can, be sure to check your nearest locations.
I've been covering pre-order events and restocks at Tom's Guide for more than five years, and know how to secure in-demand items. Below are all the links you need, alongside live updates on Zelda Switch 2 restocks.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2. One of the N64's most beloved games has been completely overhauled to celebrate the franchise's 40th Anniversary. The remake offers truly stunning visuals with 4K graphics, overhauled controls, and reworked puzzles.
I'm a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom's Guide and a more recent convert to The Legend of Zelda series. Breath of the Wild on Switch 1 was my first Zelda experience, and I can't wait to finally play Ocarina of Time.
I've been checking all the retailers every so often, but I've just done a full retailer sweep to see what's available.
A whole lot of nearly nothing.
The one place I was able to see was on Target. There's a button that will show you stores with stock near you. For me, it was one store with one console in stock about 10 miles away.
If you have gas in the car and a minute, this might be the way to get your special Switch 2.
If you didn't know there are two versions of the cover art for the Ocarina of Time remake. One with foil texture and one without.
Apparently, the retails have all swapped out the foil cover on their listings for the standard edition.
You may get lucky if you try your luck in-store, but online it appears out of stock.
GameStop is showing the Zelda console as out of stock but the Pro Controller might still be available. However, the retailer has been pushing in-store so you won't be able to get it on the website.
I called my local GameStop and they were out of stock, but you might have better luck with your closest store.
I just did a sweep through the retailers, and it looks like the only thing available is the 40th anniversary Pro Controller for $213.99 at Walmart , which is double the normal $99 price, but cheaper than what I'm seeing on Best Buy (showing as sold out).
Nothing to report at present, Target has now returned to "sold out", though perhaps we'll see a third restock later today, meanwhile no signs of any stock at Walmart so the rumors are unfortunately looking increasingly unlikely. In-store remains your chance to find a Zelda Switch 2 , so if you live locally to a retailer, it's worth trying your luck. Meanwhile, my day is winding down, but I'll be handing over to a colleague shortly, to make sure you don't miss any restocks.
Quick update on the Target situation, I'm no longer seeing the "add to cart" button, but it does direct me to "show in-store stock" with at least one location popping up claiming to have stock nearby. It would seem all the online inventory has been snapped up, but I would still recommend checking for now, you could get lucky. And Target has restocked online twice now, could it go for a third?
I didn't see this one coming, but the "add to cart" button has just returned on Target, so get over there and see if you can secure a Zelda Switch 2 as it looks like stock is returning at the retailer!
All eyes are on Walmart at present, there are rumors flying around they will restock the Zelda Switch 2 today, but so far nothing. Remember, as I keep saying, there's no confirmation here, but restock rumors often prove to have some truth to them, so fingers firmly crossed the noise around Walmart amounts to a drop.
Well, after about an hour, I'm not seeing any signs of available stock at Target, even with a lot of refreshes, so I feel pretty confident saying the retailer is once again sold out . Hopefully you were able to grab one in this latest Zelda Switch 2 restock. If not, don't worry, I'm still here tracking stock levels across retailers. Remember, Walmart is rumored to drop next.
Target was the big one today, and after restocking in the very early morning hours, I wondered if that would be the retailer sold out again, but a second restock has appeared online. The console is going to sell out fast, so get over there, and even if you get a "sold out" message at first, keep trying, as more stock could appear.
No time for talking, the Zelda Switch 2 is IN STOCK at Target, go grab yours!!!
Last night after a busy day of restock tracking, I finally got to sink my teeth into The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and while I'm very early in my quest, my first impressions are that it's a glorious remake.
Our reviewer, Anthony Spadafora, had a similar experience, calling it "even better than my childhood memories." You can read his full Ocarina of Time review if you're looking to fill some time until we have more restock news to bring you.
Rumors have been flying around this week that Walmart could restock the Zelda Switch 2 from November 6 (aka today). This is based on an unverified leak of an internal document suggesting that the national retailer was gearing up for a restock. Again, this is all unconfirmed, but it's the retailer to watch right now, and it has already this week restocked in-store, so could an online drop follow today?
One of the big themes this week has been retailers opting for in-store restocks rather than dropping stock online.
I've just checked some local Target stores, and the retailer's online tracker is telling me there is Zelda Switch 2's available at nearby locations. However it's very limited ("only 1 left"), and these in-store stock trackers aren't always updated in realtime, so even if it tells you there's stock there's no guarantees.
Still, if you've got your heart set on securing a Zelda Switch 2, and have a Target store within reasonable distance (I wouldn't recommend a lengthy roadtrip), then getting down to your nearest location might be your best chance of getting one.
It looks like Target opted for a late-night online restock based on what I've seen on social media, so if you're still on the hunt for a Zelda Switch 2, that's the place to check now. But I'm seeing conflicting reports, with some users claiming that no stock was available, so I'll keep watching the retailer for signs of more stock.
Good morning! Rory here, it's a new day, and I'm back online to track Zelda Switch 2 restock across retailers. Today (Nov. 6) is set to be a big day with at least one online restock confirmed at Target, and there could be more on the way, too.

articles.title_orig: US asks China to uphold Busan trade deal commitments ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
articles.title_zh: US asks China to uphold Busan trade deal commitments ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
articles.content_orig:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to urge Beijing to immediately implement commitments under the Busan trade agreement.
“Secretary Bessent emphasised the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments made in Busan and raised concerns about recent Chinese actions. He underscored that continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement,” the US Department of the Treasury said in a statement announcing the discussions on Friday.
The announcement refers to a trade deal negotiated between Washington and Beijing in which US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to ease tariffs and lift restrictions on tech to de-escalate tensions amid tit-for-tat tariffs imposed first by Washington and then by Beijing.
On Thursday, China said it was open to buying more US farm goods if the world’s two largest economies agreed to implement the reciprocal tariff cut.
“China has consistently been open to expanding purchases of agricultural products from the US, but only on the condition that the two sides implement their agreed ’30 billion for 30 billion’ reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement,” Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson Huang Ling said in a statement.
The move follows a September meeting between Trump and Xi, when the White House proposed $60bn in cuts, including $17bn worth of US farm goods.
In May, the White House said Beijing agreed to buy $17bn of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year’s target adjusted on a prorated basis. Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made last October to buy US soya beans.
“Secretary Bessent reiterated the Trump Administration’s commitment to pursuing trade and economic policies that benefit American workers, farmers, and businesses and strengthen U.S. economic and national security,” the Treasury added.

articles.title_orig: China to narrow scope of contentious ‘designated location’ surveillance measure
articles.title_zh: China to narrow scope of contentious ‘designated location’ surveillance measure
articles.content_orig:
Draft amendment to country’s harshest form of detention used in state security cases is sent to top legislative body for initial review
Chinese lawmakers are proposing to restrict a contentious form of detention and police surveillance measure, among other changes to the country’s Criminal Procedure Law.
Known as residential surveillance at a designated location (RSDL), the measure was originally intended as a mild restriction of personal freedoms to lower the rate of detention and arrest.
Since RSDL’s introduction in 1996 and expansion in 2012, it has become the harshest form of detention used in state security cases, including terrorism.

articles.title_zh: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested
articles.content_orig:
Late night political drama as PeÃ±a is impeached and arrested
Paraguay's President Santiago PeÃ±a has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of a digital bank with links to his private business interests.
PeÃ±a was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office due to a widening crisis triggered by the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this week.
He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached PeÃ±a and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
PeÃ±a, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The demise of the digital bank has left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions prompting widespread protests particularly in the capital, AsunciÃ³n.
The impeachment charges that led to PeÃ±a's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
PeÃ±a is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.
PeÃ±a's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
Afterwards, senate president Basilio NÃºÃ±ez said PeÃ±a was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Paraguay's Vice-President Pedro Alliana was then sworn in as interim President.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as President until 2028.
Pedro Alliana takes the oath of office as interim President
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history â a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say PeÃ±a is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".
In an address to the nation on Thursday, PeÃ±a said that he was sorry and that "it was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me".

articles.title_orig: How the US midterm elections reflected resistance to data centres
articles.title_zh: How the US midterm elections reflected resistance to data centres
articles.content_orig:
In September, a poll found that 70 percent of Democrats and 57 percent of Republicans supported limiting the construction of new data centres in the United States.
But that opposition was tested in Tuesday’s midterm election, with analysts examining key races to see if the public backlash would translate into votes.
It did. There were 41 ballot measures related to data centres in Tuesday’s midterms, spread across the country.
According to Data Centers on the Ballot, an election-monitoring project run by Redbud Consulting, voters are on track to reject data centre development in all but one of the contests.
Two of the races continue to be counted but are expected to result in majorities to reject or limit data centres.
Only Harwood, North Dakota, a small town with a population of fewer than 800 people, voted to oppose such limits. The measure it defeated would have required independent reviews of large industrial projects like data centres before they could be built in the area.
Experts say Tuesday’s midterm elections indicate that the debate around data centres has become a bipartisan issue, intertwined with cost-of-living concerns and fears over job stability.
As of April, the Pew Research Center estimated that there were already 3,000 data centres in the country, with more than 1,500 others in progress.
The construction boom has been driven in large part by the growth in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector. That industry, experts say, has fed concerns about a shifting economic landscape.
“The unchecked acceleration of AI development has been causing concern across the board,” Bhaskar Chakravorti, the dean of global business at Tufts University, told Al Jazeera.
“People worry about their jobs and what it might mean from a broader economic perspective. But closer to home, people could see the physical manifestations of AI in data centres being built in their back yards, or they were hearing about it from others.”
Not only are voters afraid that AI might replace human work, but they also fear the downstream costs of data centres, according to Chakravorti.
Data centres consume large amounts of water and energy, which critics say can drive up electricity costs for nearby communities.
“Whether higher energy costs were driven by broader factors, such as the Iran war or tariffs, AI competing for space on the electricity grid was certainly part of its unpopularity,” Chakravorti said.
Voters, he added, were seeing the results “in their energy bills”.
A 2026 working paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas estimated that, as of last year, wholesale electricity prices had risen by 6.9 percent as a result of data centres.
James Mercer, founder of Metro Colo Advisory, an independent data centre advisory firm, told Al Jazeera that those anticipated costs mobilised voters in many areas.
“What they push back on is a building down the road that needs as much power as a small city, when they suspect their own electric bill will cover it,” Mercer said.
“That’s why local resistance has grown so fast: counties pausing new projects, zoning fights and data centres turning into a ballot issue.”
That popular resistance led several candidates in high-profile races to make AI and data-centre development central to their campaigns.
Among them is Democrat Sherrod Brown , who flipped a key Senate seat in Ohio, the state that accounted for the largest share of data-centre ballot initiatives this year.
Some 21 votes were taken on data centres in the state, out of a total of 47 referendums and measures that took place across the country in 2026.
Brown, a former senator, made Republican incumbent Jon Husted’s support for data-centre development a key point of attack.
“One guy has led the charge on these. That guy’s responsible, and that’s Jon Husted,” Brown told NBC News earlier this year.
In Texas, meanwhile, Democrat Gina Hinojosa called for a moratorium on new data-centre approvals until stronger protections for local communities were put in place.
Though her position worried tech investors keen on expansion in the Lone Star State, Hinojosa ultimately defeated incumbent Greg Abbott in the governor’s race.
“While Abbott had a moratorium on data centres in Texas currently, the overriding view is this would end once he got re-elected,” Dan Ives, managing director at the bank Yorkville Ives, said in an analyst note.
“Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout, which makes worries around the future of the data center buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors.”
Another successful Democratic candidate, Senator-elect James Talarico , also flipped a Republican-held seat with a pledge to increase data centre regulation.
Texas has been at the centre of growing concerns over the water demands of AI infrastructure.
The city of Corpus Christi, for example, has faced severe drought conditions, with its reservoir falling to just 8 percent of its total capacity earlier this year.
The city has been described as at risk of running out of drinking water. Talarico proposed adopting closed-loop water systems to reduce data centre consumption. He also advocated for data centre operators to fund local infrastructure improvements.
He won Corpus Christi by a 12-percentage-point margin.
In another key Senate race, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed called for the creation of a federal agency to oversee the AI industry. He bested his Republican opponent with more than 52 percent of the vote.
With Democrats poised to control both chambers of Congress, the AI industry is likely to face increased scrutiny from lawmakers.
“[We are] more likely to get real regulation and oversight,” Alex Turner, a former researcher who resigned from Google DeepMind, told Al Jazeera.
“I look forward to advising any congressperson who wants to get serious about the risks from AI, no matter their party affiliation.”
Congressional leaders are increasingly treating AI as a national security and public safety threat, after a string of alarming security failures over the past six months.
In one incident, OpenAI autonomous agents escaped a controlled testing environment and infiltrated the tech start-up Hugging Face . In another, AI agents accessed bank accounts without authorisation, according to reporting from the publication Axios.
In late October, Anthropic’s Claude AI model also accessed voter data in Georgia.
Once the 120th Congress is sworn in on January 3, Democrats are expected to use the legislature’s oversight committees to conduct investigations into AI malfeasance.
On Tuesday night, as it became clear that Democrats would win majorities in Congress, Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts pledged that new probes were on the way.
“They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” the Democrat wrote on the social media platform X.
Another congressmember, Yassamin Ansari of Arizona, posted on social media her support for more restrictions on AI growth.
“Top of the Democratic agenda on day one needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out-of-control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence,” Ansari said.
Tech companies themselves have responded to the midterm results with proposals for alleviating voter concerns.
After the election, OpenAI published a framework titled Setting a New Standard for Responsible AI Infrastructure. In it, the company pledged to “prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling” and to “pay our own way on energy and infrastructure”.
Days before Tuesday’s contest, OpenAI also sought to rebrand its data centres as “compute campuses”.
The political shift is also hitting Wall Street. Investors increasingly see tighter oversight of AI on the horizon, and some of the sector’s biggest growth stocks have stumbled.
On Thursday, for example, chipmaker Nvidia lost $450bn in market value in a single trading day.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk Staked His Empire on Texas. Now State Democrats Want to Rein Him In.
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Staked His Empire on Texas. Now State Democrats Want to Rein Him In.
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX and Tesla shares declined by about 9% and 11%, respectively, on Thursday afternoon with investors concerned that Elon Musk could face new congressional probes — and his companies stricter regulation — following the U.S. midterm elections.
The declines, which correlated with a broader tech sell-off , brought aggregate market cap losses for SpaceX and Tesla to over $420 billion since Tuesday's close.
Musk's wealth, which had topped $1 trillion after SpaceX's initial public offering in June, is now down below $800 billion, having dropped about $90 billion in the past week, according to Forbes . He is still the richest man in the world.
Musk was the biggest donor to GOP candidates and causes in the midterms, with his financial contributions exceeding $470 million , the Financial Times first reported.
Despite his bolstering the GOP war chest, most of the candidates Musk backed lost their races .
Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. And in Texas, where both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered, Democrats Sen.-elect James Talarico and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa beat longtime Musk allies, state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott.
Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note out on Wednesday, "While policy is naturally hard to predict, we could envision SpaceX facing some incremental headwinds in this type of backdrop."
Gov.-elect Hinojosa "made data centers a major campaign issue," the analysts noted, calling for "a moratorium on new approvals until the legislature passes stronger protections on water use, electricity costs, local control, and incentives," and criticizing tax breaks for large facilities.
Tesla and SpaceX are both building out AI infrastructure in Texas, and are planning to build Terafab, a massive facility, which will include a data center and sprawling semiconductor factory, in Grimes County, Texas.
SpaceX also plans to build out a "supercomputer" at its Starbase, Texas, launch facility and company town, according to company job listings .
Deutsche Bank analysts also wrote that SpaceX's Texas compute capacity could now be at risk of delays. Capital expenditures by the company may need to increase to meet the requirements of tighter, anticipated regulations around data center buildout, the analysts wrote.
Musk and SpaceX have been instructed to preserve records concerning restrictions imposed on a military version of the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, CNN first reported , citing an aide to a Democratic senator. The restrictions hampered the country's ability to defend against attacks by Russia.
Additionally, regulatory scrutiny could block chances for Musk to merge SpaceX and Tesla, an idea he has promoted, while acknowledging shareholders' approval would be required first.
SpaceX and Tesla had lost about $456 billion in market cap by the close of business on Thursday.
-- CNBC's Nick Wells contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Hegseth calls US-Iran war a 'courageous and historic effort'
articles.title_zh: Hegseth calls US-Iran war a 'courageous and historic effort'
articles.content_orig:
Coverage for this event has ended.
President Donald Trump declined Friday to say whether the U.S. was responsible for reported missile strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, while acknowledging that American forces have conducted limited strikes against Iranian air defenses.
Asked by a reporter whether the U.S. carried out the reported strikes, Trump responded, "I don't want to talk about it. We do minor strikes, but they knock out. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five."
Iranian state media reported that two projectiles struck the Suza area of Qeshm Island, according to Reuters.
Trump did not specify where the U.S. operation he described took place or whether it was connected to the reported strikes on Qeshm Island.
President Donald Trump's top advisers are divided over whether to resume military strikes against Iran or continue negotiations, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff favor diplomacy, while Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper support renewed military operations, the newspaper reported, citing U.S. officials.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly favor maintaining economic pressure through sanctions and the blockade.
The disagreements come as Trump weighs further strikes following Republican losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. The president said Friday that Iran wants to reach an agreement with Washington.
The State Department warned Americans in the Middle East on Friday to remain vigilant amid increased threats of armed attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi militants and potential targeting of U.S. government officials.
In a security alert posted on X, the department's Bureau of Consular Affairs urged Americans in the region to exercise heightened caution and prepare for possible travel disruptions.
The department warned that Iranian-backed Houthis pose an increased threat of armed attacks and that Iran is attempting to target American government officials in the region.
U.S. citizens were also advised to monitor country-specific security alerts and remain aware of potential flight cancellations and airspace closures.
The warning comes as tensions remain high across the Middle East, with President Donald Trump weighing renewed military strikes against Iran while Washington and Tehran continue diplomatic negotiations.
President Donald Trump said Friday that Iran is eager to reach an agreement with the United States, citing economic troubles and damage to Tehran's military capabilities as Washington considers its next steps in the conflict.
During a gaggle with reporters, Trump was asked who persuaded him to pursue negotiations after launching military strikes against Iran.
"Nobody," Trump responded, defending the strikes and arguing that Iran would have posed a greater threat to Israel and other countries in the region if it had obtained nuclear weapons.
"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," Trump said.
The president also pointed to Iran's economic difficulties, asserting that inflation had reached 300% and that its navy had been destroyed.
Iran is demanding concrete action from Washington before advancing nuclear negotiations, with a senior official saying Friday that Tehran will no longer rely on written U.S. commitments.
Ali Bagheri, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, accused Washington of repeatedly violating its commitments over the past 18 months, according to state-run IRNA, as reported by Iran International.
“Iran needs to see the US’s practical actions, and [then] the groundwork for opening a new chapter would be prepared,” Bagheri said.
The remarks come as Washington reviews a nuclear proposal submitted by Tehran through Qatari intermediaries, while President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Iran.
The U.S. is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation assistance for information about Iran's nuclear program, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced Friday.
In a post on X, CENTCOM highlighted the State Department's Rewards for Justice program, which is seeking information about Iran's nuclear facilities, equipment and personnel involved in the program.
The reward also covers information about the movement of nuclear-related materials, equipment or personnel, including individuals in the scientific community.
The announcement comes as President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Iran while Washington and Tehran continue negotiations over the country's nuclear program.
Trump reiterated Friday that Iran would never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon, pointing to previous U.S. military operations targeting Tehran's nuclear facilities.
President Donald Trump reiterated Friday that Iran would never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon, pointing to previous U.S. military strikes against Tehran's nuclear facilities.
Speaking at the UP Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida, Trump credited American B-2 bombers with preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons.
"And you know what? If they did have it, if we didn't go in with those beautiful B-2 bombers a little more than a year ago, if I allowed them to have it today, there would be no Israel. It would have been wiped off the face of the earth, and there would be no Middle East," Trump said.
"We will never let that happen. Iran will never, ever have a nuclear weapon. You can rest assured," the president added.
Trump's remarks come as his administration considers renewed military operations against Iran while continuing diplomatic negotiations with Tehran over its nuclear program.
Qatar pushed back Friday against reports suggesting negotiations between the United States and Iran had collapsed, insisting that both countries are continuing efforts to reach an agreement.

articles.title_orig: Vance leads behind-the-scenes push for new Iran deal
articles.title_zh: Vance leads behind-the-scenes push for new Iran deal
articles.content_orig:
US Vice President JD Vance’s reported bid to meet Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei for peace talks with Tehran raises a troubling question for Washington: Does it understand the man it would face across the table?
For more than four decades, Rezaei has occupied positions of power from which he could make decisions that imposed extraordinary human and economic losses on Iranians, while he and his factional allies in the Islamic Republic remained largely insulated from their consequences.
Understanding this track record and how he calculates the costs of diplomacy is essential to understanding how he might negotiate with Washington, how much he is prepared to tolerate, and what could finally persuade him to compromise.
The origins of Rezaei’s cost-benefit calculus go back to 1981, when the founder of the Islamic Republic, Ruhollah Khomeini, appointed the 27-year-old Rezaei as commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The IRGC was at the time a newly established institution in which revolutionary commitment and willingness to sacrifice often carried greater weight than professional military judgment.
Rezaei flourished in that environment and, in turn, helped consolidate a command culture that treated heavy casualties as an acceptable cost of pursuing ideological or factional objectives. The relationship was mutually reinforcing, as the institution rewarded commanders willing to endure enormous losses, while those commanders perpetuated a system in which the political consequences of those losses rarely affected the people responsible for them.
That high threshold for enduring costs paid by others became particularly consequential in 1982, after Iranian forces recaptured the city of Khorramshahr and Iraq subsequently offered negotiations. As IRGC commander, Rezaei was among those who argued for entering Iraqi territory rather than halting at the border. A war begun by Saddam Hussein's invasion now became another six years of bloody battles for goals extending beyond Iran's capacity.
During the catastrophic Operation Ramadan near the port city of Basra in July 1982, Iranian troops, including forces under Rezaei's IRGC command, repeatedly attacked entrenched Iraqi positions. Historians Anthony H. Cordesman and Abraham R. Wagner estimate between 20,000 and 30,000 Iranian troops were killed or critically wounded. Some Iranian leaders nevertheless saw progress in exhausting Iraq.
One of my uncles was killed in Operation Ramadan, and another in the offensive campaigns Rezaei had advocated after Khorramshahr. In this calculation, a battlefield disaster became an investment in a hypothetical victory in the long run. That victory never came.
Iranian forces did improve tactically, as a US National Defense University study demonstrates in its account of the successful 1986 assault on Iraq’s Faw Peninsula. Yet those improvements rarely prompted Iranian commanders to reconsider whether their objectives justified the mounting human suffering and material losses, allowing the same strategic mistakes to persist even as battlefield methods evolved.
Later that year, Operation Karbala-4 proceeded despite warnings that Iraqi forces anticipated the assault and that the operation had been exposed. Thousands of mostly Iranian youths were killed, wounded or went missing. Decades afterward, Rezaei called the operation a “diversion” preceding Operation Karbala-5, before acknowledging that it began as a principal attack.
Here was another early expression of a dangerous institutional habit among Iranian decision-makers: a battlefield defeat could be treated as an investment in eventual victory, regardless of whether that victory was becoming more attainable or not.
The following year, Iranian forces continued operations toward Iraq’s Basra. A 2009 US National Defense University study, based on extensive interviews with former Iraqi Republican Guard commander Ra'ad Hamdani, described the fighting as the "Somme of the Iran-Iraq War," recalling frontal assaults with high casualties, enormous artillery concentrations and extraordinary destruction.
The National Defense University researchers concluded that repeated attacks reflected Iran’s persistent unwillingness to learn from previous failures. By 1987, they observed, Iranian political and military leaders were struggling to motivate soldiers who had suffered heavy losses without any meaningful gains.
Rezaei’s demands in the final year of the Iraq war exposed the deeper problem with his leadership style. In 1988, Rezaei set out requirements for rebuilding Iran’s offensive capacity over the following five years, including 350 infantry brigades, 2,500 tanks and 300 combat aircraft, while Prime Minister Mir-Hossein Mousavi’s government warned it could no longer finance the war.
Rezaei merely counted the weapons necessary for victory without offering a comparable accounting of the human cost of continuing the war. Ruhollah Khomeini accepted a ceasefire, and Rezaei remained commander until 1997.
Peace brought Rezaei new positions and privileges, but the wartime mentality that allowed him to accept enormous costs borne by others followed him into politics. He served as secretary of Iran's Expediency Council from 1997 to 2021 and expanded his influence beyond the military.
He ran unsuccessfully for president in 2009, 2013 and 2021, but those electoral defeats did little to diminish his access to senior positions within the Islamic Republic.
A Tehran Bureau investigation identified him as the owner of Tabnak, a major news website whose corporate structure included relatives and associates. He now had assets and networks worth protecting, even as he continued to regard sacrifice by others as an acceptable price for pursuing political objectives.
Rezaei’s response to his son’s dissent also illustrated the tension between family ties and political loyalty. Ahmad Rezaei had publicly criticized the Islamic Republic and fled the country. Mohsen Rezaei denounced him and declared that he would be treated like any dissident if he returned. Ahmad subsequently returned to Iran in 2005 and was not prosecuted, before leaving the country again.
Ahmad was found dead in Dubai in 2011. Police reported an apparent suicide, although questions persisted. Nevertheless, Rezaei's public response to his son's dissent suggested that even family ties could be subordinated to his position in a political order he had devoted his career to building.
In peacetime economic policy, the same institutional tolerance for high costs borne by Iranian citizens found another arena. Rezaei carried his understanding of costs into economics. Former associates of his presidential campaigns told me he conceived what became slain Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei's "resistance economy" and brought the idea to him.
As vice president for economic affairs under President Ebrahim Raisi from August 2021 to June 2023, he helped direct economic policy amid inflation and declining purchasing power. Once again, ordinary people financed the "resistance," while Rezaei retained his position and influence.
In an interview for this article, former Kayhan editor-in-chief and representative of Ali Khamenei Mehdi Nasiri alleged that Rezaei sought a share of Tehran’s roughly €2 billion electric-vehicle procurement deal with China under hardline Mayor Alireza Zakani in 2024, but declined to elaborate on the basis for his allegation. Separately, investigative journalist Yashar Soltani reported that the deal bypassed standard procurement procedures and involved intermediaries whose selection and financial qualifications were unclear. His report did not name Rezaei.
In August 2026, Rezaei became secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, returning to decisions over war and diplomacy. The body, chaired by President Masoud Pezeshkian, coordinates Iran's security and foreign policy. articles.title_orig: China, EU urged to deepen cooperation amid global transitions
articles.title_zh: China, EU urged to deepen cooperation amid global transitions
articles.content_orig:
China and the European Union should strengthen dialogue, manage their differences and expand cooperation in emerging areas such as artificial intelligence to ensure the stable development of their relationship over the next 50 years, Chinese Ambassador to the EU Cai Run said on Thursday.
Speaking at the 14th China-Europe Forum in Brussels, Cai said the two sides should remain committed to their partnership, resolve economic and trade disputes through consultation, and respect each other's core interests and major concerns.
"We are partners, not rivals, still less adversaries," Cai said. "China is not the source of the economic problems facing the EU, but a partner it can count on in addressing them."
The forum, themed "The Next 50 Years: Navigating Global Transitions in an AI World", was jointly organized by the Chinese Mission to the EU, Brussels-based think tank Friends of Europe and the China Public Diplomacy Association.
Cai said China-EU relations had maintained steady momentum despite challenges. According to Chinese statistics, bilateral trade reached $693.6 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 12.9 percent year-on-year, while two-way investment stock exceeded $290 billion.
He highlighted the progress achieved at the recent second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, where the two sides reached 16 deliverables and understandings covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization reform.
The two sides agreed to hold the third meeting in March next year.
"The agreement on these 16 deliverables and understandings fully demonstrates that both sides have the willingness, capability, and wisdom to resolve issues through dialogue and consultation," Cai said.
Turning to artificial intelligence, Cai said China and the EU possessed distinct strengths and should expand exchanges and cooperation to make AI a new growth area in bilateral relations while jointly advancing global AI governance.
Stefano Grassi, director for external relations at the European Commission's Secretariat-General, highlighted the deep economic ties between China and the EU, noting that China was the EU's third-largest trading partner while the EU is the first export destination for China.
Drawing on his experience during the eurozone debt crisis, Grassi said one of the most important lessons Europe had learned was that correcting economic imbalances required action from both surplus and deficit economies.
He stressed that China and the EU were highly integrated economically, and underscored the importance of jointly addressing economic challenges.
Wu Haitao, vice-president of the China Public Diplomacy Association, also emphasized the importance of dialogue in shaping the next 50 years of China-EU relations.
"Despite our differences, we are all willing to resolve them through dialogue and consultation. This is a very good starting point," Wu said, adding that "differences are inevitable, but how we resolve them matters greatly to both sides".
Against a backdrop of growing geopolitical uncertainty, Wu called on the two sides to play a constructive role in global affairs. "As two major constructive forces in the world, China and the EU should provide stability and certainty to a world marked by turbulence and change," he said.
Cai said China's commitment to high-quality development and high-standard opening-up would create new opportunities for European businesses and other international partners, expressing confidence that joint efforts would help usher in a brighter future for China-EU relations.

articles.title_orig: US East Coast could face 'cataclysmic' megatsunami from unstable Spain volcano, scientist warns
articles.title_zh: US East Coast could face 'cataclysmic' megatsunami from unstable Spain volcano, scientist warns
articles.content_orig:
An unstable island volcano in Spain’s Canary Islands could splinter and fall into the sea, creating a monstrous “megatsunami” that could wipe out the US East Coast within hours, a scientist warned.
However, when — or even if — such a disaster will strike remains an open scientific question.
Volcanologist Professor Bill McGuire has been monitoring Cumbre Vieja , a volcano, which has the potential to create a deadly transatlantic tsunami, according to an article he published in BBC Science Focus .
The growing concern centers on a massive wall of rock, also known as a “flank,” slowly inching toward the sea that would displace a biblical amount of water if it collapses, McGuire said.
“Based on extensive studies, I expect this part of the flank will eventually crash into the North Atlantic, launching a megatsunami in the process,” he wrote.
“There has been huge debate and discussion, sometimes quite heated, about the level of expected destruction, and — in particular — whether devastating waves will reach the coast of North America.”
To support the ocean-crossing potential of such waves, researchers point to massive, out-of-place boulders deposited along coastlines in the Bahamas.
Geologists believe prehistoric Canary Island tsunamis carried those rocks across the Atlantic, leaving physical evidence that the effects of flank collapses can reach across the ocean.
The worst-case scenario would be waves up to 65 feet high that could reach the Eastern Seaboard within nine hours in the event of the flank collapsing, according to McGuire’s computer simulations.
Crucially, experts stress that an Atlantic catastrophe is not imminently lurking around the corner.
While the wave itself would travel at jetliner speeds once generated, the collapse itself may not occur for centuries or even millennia.
“I have no doubt this will be a cataclysmic event, but have no idea when it will happen — it could easily be centuries or even millennia down the line,” McGuire noted.

Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion , confirmed Friday it has sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google.
Google, which Crusoe had tried and failed to land as a customer for the project, is taking over the development after reportedly raising concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe’s management.
Crusoe initially announced the project last year with Blackstone-backed infrastructure company Tallgrass, planning to eventually scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity.
Google did not disclose how much it paid Crusoe for the unfinished project, but it announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus.
The deal highlights how difficult it can be for independent data center developers to deliver massive projects on time and within budget, given the challenges of securing equipment and power. Growing opposition from local communities can further complicate development.
Despite taking over the Wyoming facility, Google hasn’t walked away from working with Crusoe entirely. Crusoe is developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas.
The deal to sell the site to Google was first reported by Bloomberg in June, but the Wyoming setback didn’t stop Crusoe from raising a $3.9 billion round in September.
Crusoe makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.
Crusoe’s largest projects serve some of the biggest names in AI. Its campus in Abilene, Texas, is being built in phases for Oracle and OpenAI, and the company is also constructing a separate 900-megawatt campus next door for Microsoft, with its first building expected to come online in mid-2027. Meta is also a customer, and Bloomberg reported that the trading firm Jane Street signed a $13 billion , five-year cloud deal with Crusoe.
Crusoe was founded by Chase Lochmiller, now its CEO, and Cully Cavness, who started it as a cryptocurrency-mining business powered by natural gas that would otherwise have been burned off. In September, alongside its $3.9 billion funding round, the company added three board members , including JB Straubel, the Redwood Materials founder and Tesla board member who invested in Crusoe in 2021. Crusoe later became the first customer of Straubel’s energy-storage business.

articles.title_orig: Russian forces launch missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, mayor says
articles.title_zh: Russian forces launch missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, mayor says
articles.content_orig:
Russian forces have launched a missile attack on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv’s mayor said, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned in his nightly video address that Russia was preparing new attacks on energy targets, bridges and other infrastructure.
Debris from Saturday’s attack damaged a residential building, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
“Explosions in the Kyiv suburbs. The enemy is hitting infrastructure with ballistic missiles,” Klitschko wrote on Telegram.
Klitschko said debris had struck a five-storey apartment building in a western district of the capital. The facade of another residential building was also damaged.
The city’s military administration said on Telegram that two people were injured and a building housing a kindergarten was damaged.
Officials continued to warn residents of the potential for more strikes hours after the attack.
The attacks come as Zelenskyy said his government is seeking specific guarantees from Western allies on how post-war security support would function. He made comments in an interview aired late on Thursday, following two days of discussions among allies in Brussels.
The talks in Brussels discussed post-war reconstruction, funding for next year and security guarantees backed by the Ukrainian government’s Western allies.
The meetings brought together officials from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and the European Union, along with representatives from the World Bank and the US investment group BlackRock, Ukrainian lead negotiator Rustem Umerov wrote in an online post.
The attacks occurred three days before US-led Ukrainian-Russian talks were to open in Abu Dhabi seeking a resolution to the war that has gone on for more than four years. The last such talks took place in February.
On Thursday, US President Donald Trump said a deal between Russia and Ukraine may be imminent , following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, at the White House.
Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday.
The meeting between the US president and Dmitriev came on the same day as First Lady Melania Trump hosted a diplomatic gathering with Russian and Ukrainian representatives to mark and build on a localised truce she helped broker in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky in October.
The truce expired last Sunday, a day before a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhia region.
The death toll from the attack has risen to 50, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said on Friday, making it one of the ⁠deadliest strikes on ⁠civilians this year.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq, S&P 500 and AI Stocks Rebound After Brutal Week
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq, S&P 500 and AI Stocks Rebound After Brutal Week
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre BaquÃ©, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: New Zealanders head to polls on final day of voting
articles.title_zh: New Zealanders head to polls on final day of voting
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand is voting in a general election against a backdrop of concerns over the rising cost of living and the broader state of the economy.
Polling stations opened at 9am on Saturday (20:00 GMT Friday) and close at 7pm (06:00 GMT Saturday).
Voting began on October 26. More than 1.6 million voters, out of nearly 3.8 million in total, had cast their ballots by the end of Thursday, according to the country’s Electoral Commission.
The country has strict laws banning any talk of politics on election day.
The 19-hour election day blackout, which ends when polling places close on Saturday evening, bars everyone, including political parties, news outlets and social media users, from commenting on likely election outcomes, campaign issues and anything else that might encourage or discourage people from voting in a particular way.
Billboards and advertising must be removed. Bumper stickers, T-shirts and even social media profile pictures are also covered by the law.
Breaches of the law can incur a fine of up to 20,000 New Zealand dollars ($11,000).
Opinion polls ahead of the tightly contested election suggest the governing centre-right National Party and the opposition centre-left Labour Party neck and neck, with neither on course to win enough seats to govern alone.
New Zealand’s Electoral Commission aims to release preliminary results from 95 percent of polling stations by the end of election night on Saturday. A final result, which will reflect ballots cast by New Zealanders abroad, is expected by November 27.
Most parties are campaigning on the economy, but their suggested solutions differ widely.
The National Party is pledging to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme.
The Labour Party is focusing on the cost of living, promising cheaper healthcare and transport.
Recent polls show no clear winner. A handful of seats either way could decide who governs.
New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional system.
Voters do not elect a leader of the country but instead select a local electorate candidate and a political party.
Electorate winners earn a seat in the typically 120-seat parliament, as do the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.

Apple introduced the Action button with the iPhone 15 Pro , and the iPhone 18 Pro still has it. Now, a tipster on Weibo claims the company is planning to combine the Action button and the Camera Control into a single button on next year's iPhones.
The dedicated Action button will allegedly start disappearing from new iPhones in the second half of 2027. Its functions will move to the Camera Control, with a single press opening the Camera app and a long press triggering the shortcut assigned to the Action button. The tipster specifically stresses that it's the Action button going away, not the camera key.
The post doesn't name any models, so it's unclear whether this would apply to the entire fall lineup or only some of it. Either way, the claim is that Apple will remove a physical button without dropping its customizable functions.
We've previously heard that next year's Pro models could feature a more substantial redesign, with quad-curved screens being tested in prototypes . Whether the rumored button change is part of that redesign remains to be seen.

articles.title_orig: Will New Zealand Join Voters’ Global Revolt Over Soaring Costs?
articles.title_zh: Will New Zealand Join Voters’ Global Revolt Over Soaring Costs?
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand is set for one of its tightest elections in years, with the incumbent conservative coalition facing an uncertain path to power and polls pointing to a millennial newcomer becoming the kingmaker.
Support for two parties that have dominated Wellington politics for almost a century – the center-right National party and center-left Labour party – has cratered below 30% respectively in public polling, with voters turning to players entrenched further to the right, the left, and to a centrist party that could enter parliament for the first time.
Frustrated with soaring living costs, stubbornly high unemployment and a stagnant economy in recent years, voters on Saturday are looking beyond their traditional choices.
Shaking up the race is the centrist Opportunity party, led by Qiulae Wong, an articulate 38-year-old former sustainable business consultant and mother of two, who goes by ‘Q’ for short. She entered politics just a year ago by responding to a job advertisement for the party’s leadership role.
Her party, pitching itself as both business- and climate-friendly and promising a land tax as well as a universal basic income to replace welfare payments, looks set to secure enough votes to cross the 5% threshold required to secure seats in parliament, on current polling.
That would make it the first total outsider party (not involving established political figures) to do so in 30 years – a “super significant” feat according to Lara Greaves, an associate professor in politics at Wellington’s Victoria University.
“There’s not been really anything like it, and we’ve seen a number of well-funded attempts,” she told CNN, explaining that the party was finding appeal with people “frustrated with the status quo.”
If Saturday’s results mirror the polls, Opportunity would hold the balance of power – with both the incumbent right and the opposition left coalition groupings in need of their support to secure a majority.
Effectively, that means Wong could have her choice of government, and her party is happy to work with either side.
But Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who leads the right-wing National-led coalition government, has already ruled out a post-election deal with Opportunity. He may yet face the stark choice of walking that back or losing power.
Neither Luxon, who faced down two caucus confidence votes on his leadership this year, nor his key opponent Labour’s Chris Hipkins (a former prime minister himself) have been able to endear themselves to the public like former leaders Jacinda Ardern and John Key.
Their relative unpopularity has shattered a decades-long trend of battle royale-style campaigns between the major party leaders, giving the minor party contenders more attention and putting them in a position to have significant influence over the direction of the next government.
Coalitions are a near constant under the South Pacific nation’s mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system, but the minor parties have traditionally been supporting players, granted a tiny proportion of cabinet posts and limited policy concessions.
The powerful position the minor parties find themselves in this year is “unprecedented territory,” says Greaves. “This is going to be the first time we’re going to see these coalition agreements where the minor parties are really going to be saying: ‘Hey, we got a big chunk of the vote. You have to stop treating us like children.’”
But that makes it “really hard to know what you’re voting for,” she said, explaining that fringe policies that get little attention during the campaign can ultimately end up on the government’s agenda after negotiations.
The incumbent National-led coalition – New Zealand’s most right-wing government in a generation – could be pushed further to the right by its emboldened partners, who have touted deepening culture war-style policies at times on the campaign trail.
For example, the right-wing-libertarian ACT party has vowed to end affirmative action schemes at the country’s medical schools, while the nationalist New Zealand First party has promised sweeping immigration changes and its populist leader Winston Peters has voiced support for a review of the ban on gay conversion therapy.
“With the 2023 government, a lot of people argue that that was already a huge lurch to the right, especially in terms of (indigenous) Māori rights … So that’s potentially concerning for more moderate voters,” said Greaves.
Conversely, parties on the right have warned voters would face a raft of new taxes if a leftist coalition were able to form a government – with Labour promising a capital gains tax, and the leftist Greens touting taxes on the “super rich” and big tech companies who take New Zealand-earned profits overseas.
“If the left bloc were to win, they would have this real concern about exactly how they get the money to do what they want to do,” said Greaves.
In recent decades, New Zealand elections have typically been easy to predict, but even the experts are struggling to foresee what voters will deliver on Saturday.
“What’s going to happen? No idea,” said Greaves.
Should Luxon’s National-led coalition lose, it will become the first single-term New Zealand government in more than half a century.

COLLEGE PARK, Md. – November 5, 2026 – IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.
“I am pleased to report that IonQ delivered its sixth consecutive quarter of record results and the strongest quarter in our company's history,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO. “Third quarter revenue of $173.8 million reflects increasing demand for our quantum technologies and the benefits of our vertically integrated quantum manufacturing capabilities through SkyWater.”
de Masi continued, “Recent developments have provided meaningful validation of our technology and commercial strategy. We are deeply proud that IonQ is the only trapped-ion company to advance to DARPA Stage C. This final stage of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative includes a potential program value of up to $300 million. In addition, NVIDIA will deploy a Superion 256 system as the first on-premise quantum computer at its Accelerated Quantum Research Center – connected directly to its AI supercomputing infrastructure. Both decisions underscore IonQ’s relentless focus on leading the industry with deployable quantum computers – built for data centers and designed to work with classical computing.”
de Masi concluded, “IonQ is building the quantum ecosystem as the first vertically integrated quantum technology company that spans computing, networking, sensing, and security. At SkyWater, we were pleased to welcome Qolab, founded by Nobel Prize winner John Martinis, as a new quantum customer. We also extended our multi-year collaboration with D-Wave and launched our OnRamp Foundry Initiative to accelerate quantum startups from laboratory prototype to commercial manufacturing.”
“One of our customers’ most urgent needs today is cybersecurity that protects them now and keeps them protected as post-quantum standards evolve. Our acquisition of Elisity extends our strategy to meet that need, adding Zero Trust technology that is both a perfect complement and accelerant to our PQC and QKD solutions. We are focused on integrating and leveraging IonQ’s differentiated solutions to drive durable growth and long-term profitability.”
Third Quarter and Recent Commercial Highlights IonQ Platform
“I am thrilled that we continued our growth trajectory in the third quarter, with revenue up 336% year-on-year. Major drivers included global deployments of our IonQ Tempo quantum computers, deliveries of our quantum sensing and space-based solutions, and closing on our acquisition of SkyWater, which had a very strong quarter of its own,” said Inder Singh, COO and CFO. “Our Remaining Performance Obligations more than doubled to $1.2 billion, even as we converted our backlog into record third quarter revenues. This was an especially strong quarter in quantum computing, which represented approximately two-thirds of new contract dollars signed by our IonQ Platform segment, driven by Superion 256 demand. We are pleased to raise our full-year 2026 revenue guidance to an industry record of more than half a billion dollars.”
Singh continued, “IonQ’s strong balance sheet, including $3.7 billion in cash and equivalents pro forma with our recent equity offering, gives us incredible financial firepower to continue investing in our technology, manufacturing infrastructure, and commercial capabilities as we scale the business and capitalize on the growing demand for quantum solutions.”

Non-GAAP Financial Measures
To supplement IonQ’s condensed consolidated financial statements presented in accordance with GAAP, IonQ uses non-GAAP measures of certain components of financial performance. Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EPS are financial measures that are not required by or presented in accordance with GAAP. Management believes that these measures provide investors additional meaningful methods to evaluate certain aspects of the Company’s results period over period.
Adjusted EBITDA is defined as net income (loss) attributable to IonQ, Inc. before net income (loss) attributable to noncontrolling interests, interest income, interest expense, income tax (benefit) expense, depreciation and amortization, stock-based compensation, executive cash-based severance, changes in fair value from recurring fair value measurements (such as warrant liabilities, contingent consideration, and investments), offering costs associated with warrants, acquisition transaction and integration costs, and non-cash legal settlements and related costs. Adjusted EPS is defined as net income (loss) per share attributable to IonQ, or EPS, excluding the impact of stock-based compensation, executive cash-based severance, changes in fair value from recurring fair value measurements (such as of warrant liabilities, contingent consideration, and investments), offering costs associated with warrants, acquisition transaction and integration costs, and non-cash legal settlements and related costs. IonQ uses Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EPS to measure the operating performance of its business, excluding specifically identified items that it does not believe directly reflect its core operations and that may not be indicative of recurring operations.
The presentation of these non-GAAP financial measures is not meant to be considered in isolation or as a substitute for the financial results prepared in accordance with GAAP, and IonQ’s non-GAAP measures may be different from non-GAAP measures used by other companies. IonQ shows a reconciliation of its non-GAAP measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures at the end of this release.
Quantum Computing and Commercial Revenue
Quantum computing revenue includes sales of our quantum computing systems and hardware, related maintenance, training, and support, consulting services, including those related to applications development, and revenue from providing access to our quantum computers through quantum-computing-as-a-service (QCaaS). Commercial revenue includes all enterprise agreements with non-U.S. government customers, including agreements with leading universities.
Remaining Performance Obligations
Remaining performance obligations (RPOs) represent the total transaction price from signed contracts that has been allocated to performance obligations that are unsatisfied (or partially unsatisfied) as of the end of the reporting period. This includes both funded (firm orders for which funding has been authorized and appropriated) and unfunded (firm orders for which funding has not yet been appropriated) portions of the contract. articles.title_orig: Companies urged to adapt as restaurant franchisee files for bankruptcy: 'Businesses want to make excuses'
articles.title_zh: Companies urged to adapt as restaurant franchisee files for bankruptcy: 'Businesses want to make excuses'
articles.content_orig:
Entrepreneur Marcus Lemonis discusses voters' feelings about their finances and taxing millionaires following the midterm elections on 'Fox & Friends.'
Companies operating in California and across the nation face growing pressure to adapt to high overhead and point to local economic conditions as the reason for financial collapse, experts say.
"A lot of businesses want to make excuses now," entrepreneur and FOX Business contributor Marcus Lemonis said Friday during an appearance on "Fox & Friends."
"What I say to business owners, small, medium and large. … ‘These are the cards we are dealt. You’re going to have to make difficult decisions.'"
MCDONALD'S DEALT LEGAL SETBACK AS JUDGE ALLOWS MCRIB MEAT LAWSUIT TO PROCEED
Lemonis noted that many companies continue to thrive in the Golden State despite high costs and strict oversight.
"If the country is going to survive the way we want it to and prosper, we're going to have to run good businesses, regardless of what state we're in," he added.
An Outback Steakhouse franchisee with 61 restaurants is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy amid piling debt, citing soaring labor costs and inflation in California. (Joshua Lott/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
Lemonis' remarks were in response to a question about San Diego–based Out West Restaurant Group, an Outback Steakhouse franchisee that filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection while pointing to California’s labor expenses and inflation as the primary catalyst for its distress.
Out West, officially known as Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, is seeking relief from a massive $449 million debt load. The company operates 61 Outback Steakhouse locations across California, Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico, a decline from the 99 restaurants it managed at its peak in 2018.
In court filings, CEO David Goronkin blamed a shrinking customer base and high operational overhead. California’s minimum wage hit $19.60 per hour in January. The filing also cited beef price increases of up to 5% annually since 2022.
"By 2026, the pressures on the business had converged," Goronkin stated in court documents. "Guest traffic and earnings continued to decline, while food, labor, and other production costs continued to rise."
MCDONALD'S HIT WITH LAWSUIT CLAIMING MCRIB CONTAINS NO REAL RIB MEAT
Out West, officially known as Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, is seeking relief from a massive $449 million debt load. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
While sit-down restaurant chains were exempt from California's $20-per-hour fast-food minimum wage law passed in 2024, full-service restaurants have faced higher labor costs statewide.
To navigate its Chapter 11 restructuring, Out West is seeking court authorization to sell its assets.
"There's a cause and effect for everything," Lemonis said. "Either I'm going to raise the prices, I'm going to cut my staff (or) I'm gonna have to close. There's always a cause and effect, and I think what these DSA candidates are gonna realize quickly is the effect is going to actually impact the people that voted for them."
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
Parent company Bloomin' Brands, which owns several restaurant chains, has agreed to purchase the remaining 61 Outback locations for $26.3 million.
The Florida-based parent company is also providing up to $5.5 million in interest-free debtor-in-possession financing.
FOX Business' Bradford Betz contributed to this report.
