articles.title_orig: A Retiree Who Bought 1,000 Oracle Shares at $39 Just Watched Microsoft Walk Away
articles.title_zh: A Retiree Who Bought 1,000 Oracle Shares at $39 Just Watched Microsoft Walk Away
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Microsoft is winding down an AI computing rental deal with Oracle. The stock hit a one-year low of $109.21, then closed up 0.8% at $116.10.
A retiree's 1,000 shares, bought for $39,090 in 2016, are worth $116,100, down from $328,330 at the September 2025 peak.
Selling 300 shares would cut Oracle from 12.7% to 8.9% of the portfolio for about $3,465 in federal tax.
Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)
Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) shareholders got one more piece of bad news on Friday. Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent artificial intelligence computing capacity from Oracle, after declining to renew the contract. Oracle stock fell as low as $109.21, down 5.2% from Thursday's close and its lowest price in more than a year. Then buyers stepped in, and the stock finished the day up 0.8% at $116.10.
That bounce does little for anyone who has owned Oracle for a while. The stock closed at $328.33 on Sept. 10, 2025. At Friday's close it was 64.6% below that peak, 40.7% lower for the year and 11.2% lower for the week alone.
Take a 66-year-old retiree who bought 1,000 shares on Nov. 7, 2016, at $39.09 a share, a $39,090 investment. Those shares were worth $328,330 at the peak. On Friday they were worth $116,100. They also collect $2,700 a month from Social Security and hold another $800,000 in retirement savings, so Oracle is now 12.7% of a $916,100 portfolio. The question in front of them is whether this week's news is a reason to sell.
The deal dates to 2023. Oracle agreed to provide Microsoft with server capacity to power a new AI-assisted version of the Bing search engine. According to Bloomberg, Microsoft has been switching that rented capacity off in recent months because the older-generation chips inside Oracle's hardware no longer fit its needs. The full size of the deal was never disclosed.
If you've saved over $1,000,000, this guide is for you. The last thing you want in retirement is to run out of money, you want your money to generate lasting income while you enjoy your life.
Now you can learn the strategies wealthy retirees use to fund their retirement with The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income from Fisher Investments. Download the guide today! (sponsor)
Oracle did not deny the report. A company spokesperson said demand for its AI cloud infrastructure "remains strong," including for earlier-generation chips, and Oracle said in September that it was renewing contracts for four-year-old chips at a 20% premium to the original price.
The report landed in a week that had already been rough for Oracle shareholders:
Monday, Nov. 2: the stock fell 8.8% after Oracle announced plans to raise $20 billion, half through new stock and half through bonds.
Thursday, Nov. 5: it fell another 6.9% as artificial intelligence stocks sold off across the market.
Friday, Nov. 6: it fell as much as 5.2% on the Microsoft report, then recovered to close up 0.8%.
Measured from the purchase, the investment still looks good. The 1,000 shares cost $39,090 and are worth $116,100, a gain of $77,010, or 197%. Oracle has also paid $12.85 a share in dividends since that purchase, or $12,850 on 1,000 shares. Today it pays 50 cents a share each quarter, $2,000 a year on this position, a yield of 1.72% at Friday's price.
Measured from the peak, the same shares have given back $212,230. That is the number that keeps most long-term holders up at night, and it is the wrong one to anchor on. The $328,330 was never cash. The decision in front of this retiree is about the $116,100 that exists today.
Oracle's business is still growing quickly. In its most recent quarter, revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion and cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% to $7.4 billion. Its backlog of signed contracts reached $664 billion.
The stock is also far cheaper than it was. At $116.10, Oracle trades at about 18 times its earnings over the past year and about 15 times what analysts expect it to earn next year. Of the 43 analysts tracked, 35 rate it a buy or strong buy, and their average price target is $235.46, about double Friday's close.
Warren Buffett's oldest rule applies here. He has quoted his teacher Benjamin Graham for decades: "Price is what you pay; value is what you get." A stock that has fallen 65% can be a better value than it was at the top, if the business behind it is still sound.
The worries are about how Oracle is paying for its growth. The company spent $55.7 billion on equipment and data centers in its 2026 fiscal year, its total debt has reached $167 billion, and analysts expect it to burn more cash than it brings in through its 2028 fiscal year. The $20 billion raise this week added more stock and more debt on top of that.
The backlog is also concentrated. According to S&P, a single AI customer accounts for about half of the $664 billion. Microsoft's decision is small next to that, but it shows that customers can and do walk away from AI computing deals that no longer fit.
For a retiree, one stock at 12.7% of everything they own is a large bet. A further 50% drop would cost about $58,000, which is almost two years of the $32,400 Social Security pays them.
Selling part of the position is a reasonable option for this retiree. If they sell 300 of the 1,000 shares at Friday's price:
Taxable gain: $23,103, since each share cost $39.09
Federal tax at the 15% long-term rate: about $3,465
What remains: 700 shares worth $81,270, or 8.9% of the portfolio, still paying $1,400 a year in dividends
If the shares sit in a traditional IRA instead of a taxable account, there is no tax on the sale itself, and the trim costs nothing today.
That keeps most of the upside if the analysts are right and cuts the damage if this week turns out to be the start of something worse. It also turns a portion of a paper gain into cash, which is the gain that actually pays bills.
Microsoft walking away from an Oracle AI deal is a real headline, and the stock's quick recovery on Friday shows the market did not treat it as a disaster. For a 66-year-old who turned $39,090 into $116,100 over 10 years and collected $12,850 in dividends along the way, the bigger question is how much of their retirement should ride on one company. Selling 300 shares would cut Oracle to 8.9% of the portfolio for about $3,465 in tax, and the remaining 700 shares would keep paying $1,400 a year.

articles.title_orig: US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions
articles.title_zh: US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions
articles.content_orig:
The United States government has announced sanctions against several Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping the Iranian regime and, in several cases, also helping the alleged head of a drug trafficking ring.
The U.S. Department of the Treasury on Friday said eight Canadian businesses had helped Iranian entities get around financial sanctions. It said some also helped launder proceeds of crime by changing Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets, like crypto.
"Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies," Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wrote in a statement.
Toronto businessman accused in U.S. of helping Iran's regime was also investigated in Canada
The sanctions effectively cut the Canadian firms off from the U.S. dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets ​the firms might have south of the border and banning any ​transactions with American people or entities.
In its statement, the treasury said the crackdown is part of a wider effort to "sever the economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime" and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which is listed as a terrorist organization in Canada .
The Treasury identified the sanctioned businesses in Ontario and British Columbia as the following:
The statement said the companies gave the Iranian regime "financial lifelines" by providing their services. In several cases, officials said the businesses have changed their names and addresses to avoid detection.
In August, the Trump administration expanded secondary sanctions its government can impose on ‌entities and countries maintaining business connections with Iran, raising the economic pressure on Tehran as the war neared its six-month mark.
"​Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran ⁠stands alone," Bessent said at the time.
Trump administration expands U.S. sanctions on Iran targeting countries with business ties to Tehran
In addition, the statement said three of those businesses helped Ryan Wedding — the Olympian-turned-alleged-drug-kingpin — hide money by laundering bulk cash into digital assets. Ultimately, the treasury said companies sent millions of dollars worth of digital funds abroad before Wedding was arrested in January .
CBC News has contacted Wedding's lawyer for comment.

Her work over the past decade has taken her across North America, from the Canadian Rockies to Washington, D.C. She routinely covers the Canadian courts, with a focus on precedent-setting civil cases. You can send story tips to rhianna.schmunk@cbc.ca.

articles.title_zh: The Fastest Production Car In The World Just Broke 310 MPH On A Public Road
articles.content_orig:
Was it really that long ago when 200 mph was the top speed for supercars? That’s 320 km/h, a speed that was attainable for cars such as the Ferrari F40 and the RUF CTR Yellowbird in the late 1980s. Nearly twenty years later, in April 2005, a Bugatti Veyron 16.4 broke 400 km/h and 250mph, and it was a fearsomely powerful car with over 1000 horsepower from its quad-turbo, eight-liter W16 engine.
These days, the big number is 500 km/h (310 mph). It took a Chinese manufacturer to break the 500 km/h barrier for production cars, and the vehicle in question is a Yangwang U9 Xtreme, a 3,019-horsepower electric hypercar.
Yangwang has been chasing these immense speeds for years, and progress has been relatively quick. Back in January 2024, the non-Xtreme Yangwang U9 did 309 km/h (192 mph) in airport runway tests in its homeland, achieving 391 kmh (240 mph) at the Auto Testing Papenburg track in Germany in October of the same year.
The Yangwang U9 is a 1300-horsepower, quad-motor, all-wheel-drive (Yangwang calls it ”individual-wheel-drive”) hypercar that hits 62 mph in 2.36 seconds. And the Xtreme… well, it’s an extreme version of that, and is the most powerful production car in the world at the moment. It’s a production car in the sense that 30 cars, which are already allocated, will be built for Chinese customers who have been invited to buy it, and it is street legal and homologated in China.
First of all, the Xtreme’s four electric motors produce 755 horsepower each, for a total output of over 3,000 horsepower. That’s a power-to-weight ratio of 1,217 horsepower per ton, as it weighs around 2,500 kg (5500 lbs), making it heavy for a supercar or hypercar.
Compared to the U9, the U9 Xtreme uses a 1200-volt architecture instead of an 800-volt one, and is the first production car with a 1200V system. (For example, a Hyundai Ioniq 5 is an 800V car, while a Tesla Model S is a 400V car.) There aren’t even fast chargers set up to take full advantage of the car’s 1.2-kilovolt architecture, but since the battery is a regular-size 80kWh LFP battery, charging it must feel instantaneous at 500kW speeds.
The U9 Xtreme came close to hitting 500 km/h already a year ago. It did 472 km/h in August 2025 and 496 km/h in September, meaning it broke 300 mph on the latter attempt. These runs were done on test tracks, but the new record speed run on November 1 was done on a public highway in Abu Dhabi, naturally without any other traffic sharing the road.
The exact speed achieved on November 1st was 503.17 km/h, or 312.66 mph. Guinness World Records and the global governing body for motorsport, FIA (Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile), confirmed the speed, making the U9 Xtreme the world’s fastest production car and the fastest production electric vehicle. Behind the wheel was Mark Basseng, a German racing driver who won the GT1 class world championship in 2012, driving a Mercedes-Benz SLS AMG GT3.
Importantly, the earlier 496 km/h speed wasn’t considered eligible for a speed record, as a vehicle needs to be tested in both directions within one hour, according to Guinness rules. The new record run was done in two directions.
The Yangwang team had the six-mile road for themselves for two days. The stretch of highway E11 was cleaned and inspected for any debris, first to get the desert sand off, and then to see if the cleaning equipment had left anything on the surface.
You might want to pause there and think about how much 300 mph even demands of the tires. The manufacturer states the tires were specially developed semi-slicks, and the rim surface was treated with a high-viscosity product to prevent the wheels spinning inside the tires during acceleration or braking. The tire manufacturer in this case is Giti Tire, which you might know as GT Radial brand tires.
When Top Gear took a Veyron to 253 mph , James May noted that the Bugatti’s tires would last only fifteen minutes at the car’s top speed. Tire technology must have advanced by leaps and bounds in twenty years, but doing 300 mph must still eat the tires up fairly quickly.
During tests done in preparation for the Abu Dhabi record run attempt, a U9 Xtreme crashed into a barrier at a reported 360 km/h (over 220 mph). Despite the immense speed and the number of parts and debris thrown around the track, the passenger cell appeared to have remained intact, and the test driver reportedly exited the vehicle on his own.
In the article by Car News China , we see the rear axle ripped out, and it’s worth noting the vehicle did not catch fire in the accident. It also shows how important aerodynamics are at these kinds of speeds, and why the car’s aero was carefully honed to reach 500 km/h after previous attempts.
To improve control and stability, the U9 Xtreme utilizes an active suspension setup, which Yangwang calls the DiSus-X. The system features electronically controlled two-valve shock absorbers, which are adjusted individually on the go. Combined with the individual wheel drive system adjusting each wheel’s torque over a hundred times per second, the U9 Xtreme’s body control sounds state-of-the-art, even if it couldn’t prevent the aforementioned crash. Yangwang claims the vehicle can lean into corners like a motorcycle as it overcomes body roll.
Yangwang hasn’t yet confirmed a sales price for the production U9 Xtreme hypercars, but while the “base” U9 is priced at around $250k in China, the Xtreme can cost several times that. Or as a BYD Accessories blog puts it :
Any website publishing an exact Xtreme price tag without citing an official Yangwang source is guessing. Given the 30-unit production cap and the race-bred engineering (1200V platform, titanium carbon-ceramic brakes, bespoke semi-slick tires), industry estimates place the Xtreme between USD 400,000 and USD 700,000. The standard U9 at USD 252,630 is the only figure confirmed by Yangwang directly.
The in-car video is great: you can see the road is a relatively regular-issue stretch of eight-lane highway, and the record speed arrives without much drama. The Yangwang sits in the leftmost lane, and just imagine a solitary SUV drifting in your lane when you’re doing 300mph.
Will we ever see the U9 Xtreme outside China, after the record run? Given that the Dubai police force recently received a Yangwang SUV for its PR fleet, Dubai’s certainly a place where one could expect to spot one of these.
Forget how long the tyres last at that speed, how long does the battery last when going 503 km/h?
As many have said here, its ridiculous and more or less unusable in many contexts (maybe they should do Bonneville) the tech is valuable. Record on Sunday-ish, sell on Monday. This is better than a flying car that really looked to be hovering
That Yang sure seems to have some wang to back it up.
Here is to hoping Giti tire starts making a cheap super 200 for America that is competitive with the current top of the crop as those tires are too expensive and don’t last long enough. Vitour has recently done something similar, being an unknown to quickly setting serious lap times. Also, basically anyone running on a track with 200 tw or stickier tires runs into the whole “tire slipping on the rim” thing during braking and accel, it’s why drag cars have beadlocks and why a lot of road course cars don’t even put weights to balance wheels/tires as the tire will immediately move and just make any imbalance worse with the added weights.
They should use the technology to make condoms. I tend to experience the same issue during acceleration/deceleration. I still manage some really fast runs though.
I look forward to this topping 550 km/h when it’s available as a rental.
Record setting hypercars have grown tedious.  Even on track you won’t hit these speeds – and heaven help the rest of the population if some gazillionaire decides to try this on a public road.
Genuinely beneficial darwinism. In a truly just world, this and the Tesla Roadster would both be in production.

articles.title_orig: Seeds and preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
articles.title_zh: Seeds and preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
articles.content_orig:
Ancient humans were using cannabis far earlier in history than we thought
New findings from a Siberian tomb offer the earliest direct evidence for human marijuana use
By Mary Randolph edited by Claire Cameron
Join Our Community of Science Lovers!
Whether you’re eating, smoking or drinking it, cannabis is commonplace; in the U.S., more people use it on a daily or near-daily basis than any other intoxicating substance, including alcohol or cigarettes. But how far back does humanity’s relationship with cannabis stretch?
In new research, archaeologists have dated the earliest known human use of cannabis to 2,800 years ago. The drug was likely used in a burial ritual at a tomb discovered in what is now Siberia . The archaeologists found direct evidence of its use, gathered from a combination of seeds and human hair—together these provide new insights into ancient societies and their cultural legacies’ potential influence on our world today, experts say.
“There is a lot of speculation about the use of psychoactive substances in the past,” says Gino Caspari, the paper’s lead author and an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany. “It is extremely rare to find real evidence for it. We bring a bit of realism into these debates, and we show that cannabis has a deep cultural history which might factor into ongoing societal discourse on legalization and medical use.”
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Caspari’s team excavated Tunnug 1, a burial mound used by the Scythian people in southern Siberia that dates to between the eighth and ninth centuries B.C.E. While studying the tombs, the archaeologists found more than 1,000 cannabis seeds. Radiocarbon analysis dated them back to the early eighth century B.C.E.
The real breakthrough, though, was in the human hair recovered from the burial sites, Caspari says. It contained cannabinol, a chemical produced from tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC—the compound that makes cannabis psychoactive.
“We had our suspicions when the little seeds first appeared in the tomb, but when we spotted the netlike pattern on the surface, this was a real moment when we knew we were holding something very special in our hands,” he says. “A little later we saw that there was also preserved human hair in the same burial—that was almost too good to be true.”
Researchers already knew that humans have a long history with cannabis. People have been cultivating the plant for agricultural reasons for at least 6,000 years. Until now, the earliest evidence of cannabis use dated to around 2,500 years ago: charred marijuana remains found in eastern China that contained high levels of THC. That evidence, however, was indirect because it only showed the plant remains—whereas the newly found combination of seeds and human hair offers a “smoking gun of evidence” for humans using the plant to get high, says Casper Meyer, an archaeologist at Bard College, who was not involved in the new study.
Meyer says that the finding challenges our modern assumptions of religion, drugs and the intersection of the two.
“It’s an interesting way of looking at what ritual can be, what religion can be, and how it can bring people together,” he says. “There’s also a rethinking of what intoxication in a communal context is.”
Because the Scythian culture had no written language, researchers must rely on sites such as Tunnug 1 for clues to the people’s empire, which spanned from as early as the ninth century B.C.E. to as late as the third century C.E. and across the Asian continent.
As archaeologists continue to uncover the site, there will certainly be more plants that reveal secrets of these steppe societies, says William Taylor, an archaeologist at the University of Colorado Boulder, who was also not involved in the new work.
“It’s easy to look at this stuff and say, ‘Oh, the Scythians toked the reefer,’” Taylor jokes. “But in fact, it is a tremendously powerful snapshot into an interconnected world in which the people and cultures of the steppe were starting to shape life on both ends of a massive continent.”
Cannabis can often carry stigma or exist on the outskirts of research, Taylor says, but the new evidence, published today in Science, “fills this really important gap in our understanding of human history.”

articles.title_orig: Re-releases of Wing Commander, Ultima titles hit Steam and GOG
articles.title_zh: Re-releases of Wing Commander, Ultima titles hit Steam and GOG
articles.content_orig:
Many people are not big fans of game publisher EA right now for good reason , but for those who remember a better time in the 1990s, there’s a little good news. Twenty-five classic games from that EA era have been lightly remastered and updated, then placed for sale on Steam and GOG , including several Wing Commander games and nearly the entire Ultima series.
Below is the full list of remastered or re-released games:
In a lengthy blog post published this week, Jim Vessella, a senior producer at EA, described the efforts that went into remastering Wing Commander I-IV and Prophecy , Privateer 2 , and Road Rash .
It’s a long, detailed story that’s worth reading yourself, but here’s a top-level summary. After working on the mostly widely acclaimed Command & Conquer: Remastered Collection in 2019, Vessella writes that he learned about and visited a room at EA’s Redwood Shores campus that contained a large archive of poorly labeled or sorted physical media from ages past.
In his free time, and with the help of others, he began cataloging this archive and discovered, among other things, that it contained virtually the entirety of the original masters of Wing Commander III and Wing Commander IV ‘s full-motion-video cutscenes.
The story that ensues involves building a small team of contractors, poring through the footage 17 hours a day on swing shifts to label and digitize it, and then coordinating with several key community members—particularly Matt Wells, who has made community enhancement patches for some of the Wing Commander games—to put together remasters of those games.
The flagship offering of those remasters is much, much higher-quality full-motion video sequences than have ever been available before, but other enhancements include 60 frames-per-second gameplay, a plethora of newly available .INI tweaks, and full controller support (though looking at the Steam forums for the games, some folks are having trouble with said controller support).
For Privateer 2 —the little-remembered sequel to Wing Commander: Privateer —the crew couldn’t find the original, high-quality remasters of the FMV scenes, and ended up getting in touch with the game’s original cinematics director, Steve Hilliker, who had the tapes in his attic. Hilliker had always wanted to take a new color-grading pass, and he did just that, while also remastering and upscaling all of the cutscenes.
Similar updates were given to Wing Commander Prophecy . The blog post also details GOG’s involvement in restoring and remastering Prophecy and Road Rash . For the latter, EA re-licensed the entire original soundtrack for re-release.
The e collection is on sale on GOG and Steam right now; previous owners of the old versions of the games on GOG and the EA storefront get these remasters for free. None of the games cost more than $5 each.
One good story doesn’t undo a lot of bad news and questionable decisions from EA, but this shows that a few passionate people can do something remarkable for game preservation, even if some of the work was done on a volunteer basis outside normal working hours. (EA committed some resources to the restorations as the project progressed, though.)
While the remasters aren’t perfect, the gaming industry could use news like this. It’s worth reading the full story in the blog post for a journey down memory lane and a look at how involved a restoration process like this can be.

articles.title_orig: Hands-On With Apple's New OLED Touchscreen MacBook Pro
articles.title_zh: Hands-On With Apple's New OLED Touchscreen MacBook Pro
articles.content_orig:
Happy touch your Mac day! Apple's new PROLED MacBook Pro is now in the hands of customers. We picked up one of the new machines to get our greasy fingerprints all over that pristine OLED display.
The ‌OLED‌ display is the major new feature, and it looks as good as you would expect from a display in a laptop starting at $2,899. Blacks are true black, and since each pixel lights up individually, there's none of the bloom you get with mini-LED when viewing bright objects on a dark background. The PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ can get super bright too, and that brightness paired with the deep blacks, HDR content looks great. ‌OLED‌ sometimes isn't bright enough outdoors, but that's not the case here.
The display bezels are thinner, and the 16-inch machine is actually 16.3 inches instead of 16.2. There's also an iPhone-like Dynamic Island that replaces the notch and houses Siri AI, Live Activities, and more. The ‌Dynamic Island‌ makes sense because you can now touch the ‌MacBook Pro‌'s display. It works like touching an iPhone or iPad , so you can swipe through webpages, tap buttons, drag and drop, and pinch to zoom.
Touch isn't meant to replace the trackpad and keyboard, but it's there if you want it. Apple made some tweaks to macOS, so menu options expand a little more when you touch them than when you click them, and tiny window resizing buttons get larger. Apple put a sturdier hinge in the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ so the display won't move as much when you tap it, but it's not perfect. It does still jiggle depending on where you tap.
The touch feature is fine, but it's probably not a reason to go out and get the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌. It has the potential to be useful in some situations, but it's not going to dramatically change the way most people use a laptop.
New chips weren't ready in time for the PROLED machines, so they use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max as the mini-LED models. That's a disappointment in a laptop that starts at almost $3,000. Since Apple is still selling the mini-LED models, you're basically paying a $400 premium for the higher-end ‌OLED‌ display, the thinner and lighter design, and the touch functionality.
The better display and the lighter weight are going to be worth the price for some people, and the touch is just a bonus.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV, who had cancer surgery just weeks ago, begins grueling South American tour
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV, who had cancer surgery just weeks ago, begins grueling South American tour
articles.content_orig:
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT — Three countries in 12 days, a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses on a trip covering around 19,000 miles. Less than a month after Pope Leo XIV underwent cancer surgery , he set off on what the Vatican called a “homecoming” tour of South America.
The 71-year-old’s long trip across the strongly Catholic region will take him to Uruguay and Argentina, as well as to Peru, where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.
Leo considers the tour, one of the most grueling undertaken by a Catholic leader in decades, a “homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected,” Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni told journalists at a briefing Tuesday.
The Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday that he was ⁠hoping to “strengthen the faith, renew hope” and “rekindle the fire of charity.”
Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by ​Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details.
Bruni said the pope would also address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, ⁠arms trafficking and regional political instability, bringing “a message of communion and unity.”
Leo departed from Rome’s Fiumicino Airport early ​Friday, and arrived in Uruguay on Friday afternoon for the country’s first papal visit since 1988.
After takeoff, Leo told journalists aboard the plane that he had no doubt he would embark on the trip.
“I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place. I confess that from the first day I had no doubt,” he said. “I was convinced that this trip had to go forward and very happy to say, praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistants, I am here today, I think, in fairly good shape.”
Asked if he had any advice for other people facing cancer, Leo replied, “Not to be afraid, early detection is obviously the best way to go, regular check ups and take care of yourself.”
Leo also noted that “trust in God, good doctors, good surgeons, and, overall, a healthy lifestyle” had contributed to his quick recovery.
Leo, who is the first pope to vote in a U.S. election, was also asked about the importance of voting.
“I am proud to be an American and to exercise my right,” he said.
Considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people go to Mass regularly, Uruguay was the first in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use and the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion.
In October 2025, the country of just 3.5 million people became the first in the region to approve legislation for assisted dying despite strong opposition from the Catholic Church.
After Uruguay, Leo’s tour will take him to Argentina for three days, where he is expected to meet with right-wing President Javier Milei , a close ally of President Donald Trump .
It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since Pope John Paul II traveled to the country in 1987.
Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was born in Argentina, the first pontiff from the region, but he declined numerous invitations to return to his homeland.
The biggest crowds of the trip are likely next week during his six-day visit to Peru, where Leo is widely celebrated as a beloved national figure. He will stop off in the capital, Lima, before visiting his former diocese of Chiclayo, where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until taking up a Vatican post in 2023.
Leo, who was treated last month for lung ‌adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, will also make several high-altitude visits in the Peruvian Andes.
Doctors have ⁠said that the disease was localized and that he would not require any further treatments; Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures ⁠would be necessary during his trip.
Speaking at the same briefing Tuesday, Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief, said Leo was grateful for the concern about his health and the demands the journey might make on him.
But, she said, he was “so excited” to make the trip.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: US labor market regains ground as job growth surges, unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.title_zh: US labor market regains ground as job growth surges, unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.content_orig:
Americans who lose their jobs these days are facing a harsh new problem: It's getting harder to find another one quickly.
The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to Friday's jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That amounts to a job search of nearly seven months, the longest outside of the pandemic period since 2016, when the U.S. labor market was finally getting back on track after the 2008 financial crisis.
About 2 million Americans have been without work for at least 27 weeks, the BLS reported. People in this category are referred to as the "long-term unemployed " and accounted for 27.6% of all jobless workers in October, the highest share since late 2021.
"This is a series that can be noisy from month to month," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed, a hiring platform. "But if you look over a longer time horizon, there is no mistake in the trend."
It's a troubling sign in an otherwise steady labor market. Workers stuck on the sidelines are a casualty of what's become a "low-hire, low-fire" job market, in which companies are hesitant to lay workers off, but aren't adding them either.
Research shows that Americans who experience long-term unemployment face depleted savings, lower earnings potential over time and declining mental health.
What's more, workers who are unemployed for extended periods risk falling into a self-perpetuating cycle, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond wrote earlier this year .
"Time spent unemployed may itself reduce the probability of finding a job, perhaps because skills depreciate, networks thin or employers interpret long unemployment durations as a negative signal," the researchers warned.
Workers stop being able to claim most, if not all, government unemployment benefits after 26 weeks in a year. Given that, a rising share of long-term unemployed people can explain in part why initial and continuing jobless claims have remained low.
"Now, the average unemployed person takes longer to find a job than their benefits would last," Stahle said. "That is a really key point of this."
While jobless workers appear to be having a tough time, this week's employment data shows strength in other areas of the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls blew past economists' forecasts for October and added 165,000 jobs, according to Friday's release. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, slightly lower than economists predicted.
Job openings came in much higher than economists expected in September, according to a separate report from the BLS released on Tuesday. The number of workers quitting jobs — a barometer of their confidence to obtain new employment — spiked to levels not seen since March 2025.
The BLS also said layoffs and discharges dropped to their lowest volume in more than a year. However, a recent string of high-profile workforce cuts could throw cold water on views among workers that the market is heating up.
CNBC reported this week that Disney is planning to axe thousands of jobs , the latest of several waves of layoffs at the media giant this year. American Express said last month that it was slashing head count by 5% as it reorients around artificial intelligence.
"It's difficult to separate what's happening to you or the people around you from the big picture," said Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360. "When your LinkedIn is filled with layoffs and your social circle features a few folks who have been job seeking for several months, positive narratives about the labor market can seem jarring."

articles.title_orig: Russian ballistic missiles slam Kyiv after Zelensky warns of mass attack
articles.title_zh: Russian ballistic missiles slam Kyiv after Zelensky warns of mass attack
articles.content_orig:
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Several waves of Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv overnight on Nov. 6-7, just hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia was preparing another large-scale infrastructure attack.
At least two people in the city of Kyiv have been wounded, along with a third victim in the surrounding region, according to authorities.
As Ukraine's Air Force warned that ballistic missiles were bound for the capital, a series of explosions rocked the city, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
The first barrage of missiles attacked Kyiv in quick succession, with the Air Force reporting that at least six missiles were launched at the city in the span of a few minutes shortly before 11 p.m. local time on Nov. 6.
Residents received an all-clear signal about 30 minutes later. But the respite was brief, with another aerial alert coming shortly before midnight. A fresh missile wave targeted the city shortly after 1 a.m., with Kyiv Independent journalists reporting another round of at least six loud blasts.
At least two people have been injured, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration. The victims are receiving medical treatment.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported explosions in the suburbs and warned that Russia was attacking infrastructure facilities with ballistic missiles.
Later, the mayor reported damage to a five-story residential building in the city's Solomianskyi district and shattered windows at another five-story building at an unspecified location. Emergency services have been dispatched to both scenes, he said.
A fire also broke out at a non-residential building in the Solomianskyi district, the Kyiv City Military Administration said . A kindergarten in the same district was also damaged by the attack.
Explosions again rocked the city at 3:04 a.m. local time, a Kyiv Independent journalist on the ground reported.
The wave of explosions continued with ballistic missiles targeting the city at 3:30 a.m. local time, a reporter said.
The full extent of the consequences is not yet clear. Attacks remain ongoing at the time of publication.
Outside of the city, Kyiv Oblast Governor Tymur Tkachenko reported that a Russian jet-powered drone attack in the Brovary district caused a fire in a home, injuring one victim. Earlier in the evening, Zelensky told Ukrainians that intelligence reports point to another massive Russian strike on infrastructure. The attack will likely target bridges, energy facilities, and civilian infrastructure, he warned.
Kyiv, a city the size of Berlin with a population of 3 million, has come under relentless assault in recent weeks as Russia begins its annual campaign against Ukraine's power grid. The city endured the largest strike on energy this year on Nov. 3, leading to widespread blackouts and water supply cutoffs.
As residents suffer, city officials and the central government have traded blame for the worsening state of Kyiv's energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
Ukraine struck various sites in the Russian regions of Oryol, Saratov, and Rostov, hitting an oil refinery among several targets overnight on Nov. 7, monitoring channels reported.
At least three people have been injured in the city and the surrounding region. Damage has been reported at homes, apartment buildings, and a kindergarten.
"In hindsight, it was a mistake for SpaceX to send (Ukraine) thousands of free Starlink dishes and millions of dollars a month in free service at the beginning of the war," the post reads.
"In general, we are more optimistic for cooperation between the U.S. and Ukraine," David Arakhamia, head of Zelensky's parliamentary faction, told reporters on Nov. 6.
The talks in Abu Dhabi are expected to take place in a trilateral format, with Ukrainian, Russian, and U.S. officials in attendance.

Two suspects can be heard discussing physically assaulting Denys Bihus or dousing him with acid, in an attempt to intimidate the founder of Bihus.info, an outlet known for investigating high-level corruption, according to NABU tapes.

All interagency regional teams will now follow the same rules for examinations, forensic medical studies, collection of biological samples and documentation, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more
articles.content_orig:
This week, Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta. The update includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 …
As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo . That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.
Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:
So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.
The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.
The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.
For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 users, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.
For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.
As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.
For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support . This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left to make it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.
Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.
iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.
When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.
This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.
iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains :
We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.
There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.
With iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:
Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.
While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple says it will start shipping to customers in a few months.
iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.
iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:
iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari . First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.
iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.
For Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.
The update also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

articles.title_orig: Investors try to regain their footing after tech stocks tank
articles.title_zh: Investors try to regain their footing after tech stocks tank
articles.content_orig:
Tech stocks in the U.S. steadied Friday after suffering one of their worst routs in years, as investors weighed the prospect of an AI investment slowdown resulting from Democratic midterm victories against the sector’s long-term growth potential.
The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 closed up 1.1% after plunging 6.3% on Thursday, its worst single-day performance since the Covid-19 pandemic.
The broader S&P 500 finished 0.3% higher, after tanking 4.4% Thursday, a drop that wiped out $2.8 trillion worth of wealth on paper.
A strong October jobs report Friday morning increased the odds that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its next policy meeting in December. The prospect of higher borrowing costs helped to push stocks down from their highs earlier in the day.
Investors continue to digest the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which a crop of Democratic candidates were elected to office who had pledged to rein in AI and data centers . They include Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas, a state that is among the largest data center markets in the country.
The AI boom is responsible for an ever-increasing share of U.S. stock market gains and economic growth, so any threat to the narrative of demand-fueled growth can rattle investors.
“Markets are being punished according to their dependence on the U.S. AI infrastructure cycle,” Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Singapore-based SAXO Markets, told NBC News.
The incoming Democratic-controlled Congress could also tighten scrutiny of the AI industry, including its infrastructure projects, which could cause delays and additional costs.
This would add to existing worries investors already have about the long-term profitability of these investments.
Some analysts viewed Thursday’s dramatic sell-off as overblown —  merely a sign of some froth coming off an overstretched market —  rather than the end of the line for the AI investment boom.
Recent declines are “just speed bumps,” said economist and investor Ed Yardeni.
Rather than spelling doom for the sector, Yardeni said losses like this week’s could ultimately help keep the AI bubble from overheating.
Until it becomes clearer how much data center construction is truly threatened by newly elected lawmakers, volatility is likely to continue.
“This is a stock market that is trying to figure out the right valuations for the AI trade, which is grappling with a swift sentiment shift after the midterm elections,” said Alex Guiliano, chief investment officer at New Jersey-based Resonate Wealth Partners.
Friday kicked off with steep losses in Asia. Japan’s Nikkei suffered its worst week since 2020, falling as much as 6% and more than 20% since its most recent high, putting it in bear-market territory. South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled more than 8%, triggering a temporary market-wide trading halt. There, AI data center memory suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix plunged more than 10% in the early hours, before recovering some of their losses.
In Taiwan, home to some of the most critical AI companies, including chip supplier TSMC, the benchmark TAIEX index dropped 9%.
The companies in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan are linked to the global AI spending cycle and “hence I am not surprised to see the magnitude of correction today following the sharp correction in the U.S.,” Tai Hui, J.P. Morgan’s APAC chief market strategist, told NBC News in emailed comments.
The months leading up to the American elections had already been a rollercoaster for Asian investors, who saw their fortunes soar in June during the AI stock boom, but have been suffering from a brutal recent sell-off.
A sense that valuations of key AI companies were inflated was troublesome enough for markets in Asia, but the Democratic sweep has introduced another layer of uncertainty.
Markets had largely expected losses for Trump’s Republicans, but not on this scale.
“This matters enormously for Asia because much of the hardware supporting America’s AI ambitions is manufactured here,” Chanana, from SAXO Markets, said.
In China, both the tech-focused Star 50 and the AI Index slumped as much as 5% before recouping some losses.
“There is a legitimate argument that parts of China’s AI equity bubble have already burst,” Chanana said.
But she added that unlike the U.S., where much of the investment is commercially driven, “China treats AI and semiconductor self-sufficiency as strategic national priorities.”
“This means investment can continue for reasons beyond immediate profitability, including technological independence, industrial competitiveness and national security.”
That is not the case in South Korea, whose market darlings, memory makers SK Hynix and Samsung, are an integral part of the commercial AI buildout. That makes the country particularly sensitive to any U.S. slowdowns.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index more than doubled in market value in June, but by Friday had shed most of the gains made this year. Like South Korea, there is acute exposure for Taiwan — key for advanced chip manufacturing and TSMC’s headquarters.
Nevertheless, most of the Asian indexes are still higher than they were a year ago: South Korea’s Kospi is up 25%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 is up 13%, and TSEC Taiwan Technology is also up by 47%.
“For semiconductor and memory makers in Asia Pacific, as long as global demand for computing power continues to grow, demand for the underlying hardware should remain healthy over the medium term,” J.P. Morgan’s Hui said.
“There may be constraints on where the ‘gold’ can be mined, but as long as demand for the gold remains, the picks and shovels will still be needed elsewhere,” he added.
Mithil Aggarwal is a Hong Kong-based reporter/producer for NBC News.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Three men charged in US with using AI to impersonate CEOs and steal millions
articles.title_zh: Three men charged in US with using AI to impersonate CEOs and steal millions
articles.content_orig:
Men allegedly impersonated voices and images of executives to convince employees to send large payments
Three foreign nationals were arrested and charged with using AI to allegedly impersonate corporate CEOs and attorneys to steal over $100m, according to an indictment that was newly unsealed by the US Department of Justice.
According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men – Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit – were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026.
With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money.
The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. The men allegedly stole nearly $5m from a hospital system headquartered in Missouri; about $2.7m from a Rhode Island bank, about $3m from a California hospital system, over $4.6m from a mutual fund headquartered in Massachusetts and about $5m from a pet food company in Florida. The men also stole over $11m from a UK tech company.
The men would direct employees to wire money to bank accounts all over the world including in the United States, Spain , Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China. After the money had been wired, the men would covert the money into cryptocurrency “in an attempt to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the stolen proceeds and distributed it amongst themselves and their co-conspirators”, according to the DoJ press release. Soall and Hazan went by several aliases: Soal’s nicknames included “Seba Clarke” and “Rocky Balboa,” while Hazan went by “Superman Cash,” “Fat Boy,” and “Ron.”
In a statement, Jamie McDonald, a US attorney, said artificial intelligence had great potential but that the public should recognize that some may seek to use the technology to pursue criminal goals.
“The alleged scheme orchestrated by Soall, Hazan, and Sheetrit demonstrates how the use of advanced technology can be exploited to commit large-scale fraud,” said James C Barnacle Jr, the FBI assistant director in charge, in a statement. “As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities.”
The men have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, various counts of money-laundering conspiracy and aggravated identity theft.

articles.title_orig: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
articles.title_zh: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre BaquÃ©, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love
articles.title_zh: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love
articles.content_orig:
The watchOS 27.3 beta adds Live Rewind and Siri Recap to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
The watchOS 27.3 beta adds Live Rewind and Siri Recap to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
It’s impossible to paint a full picture of what Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will be right now. The watchOS 27.3 developer beta just dropped earlier this afternoon, and these features are meant to be lived with in day-to-day life. We’re definitely going to do that over the next few weeks at The Verge . That said, here are some initial impressions.
What’s newly available today is Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds, while the latter provides high-level summaries of your conversations. (The other two Audio Intelligence features have been available for the last few weeks. I wrote about those in my Series 12 review .) And as always, this is the developer beta. These features could still change quite a bit before a final version arrives for the public.
The first thing I noticed is that these features are not turned on by default. I wasn’t expecting anything different, but it’s worth remembering that these features don’t automatically turn every Apple Watch into a surveillance device. Audio Intelligence requires the latest Apple Watch hardware, a compatible version of iOS (so in this case, the iOS 27.3 developer beta), and someone has to actively choose to enable these features. You can download the beta and double-press the crown to initiate a Live Rewind. It won’t do anything. You must opt in via your iPhone’s Watch app. Same goes for Siri Recap. Enabling Live Rewind also requires an initial microphone calibration with your phone.
Privacy-wise, Apple has publicly available support documentation about its approach to these features. I’m not weighing in on how well it executes them in this hands-on. But Apple has pretty clear messaging in the onboarding process. There are quite a few customization options for when Siri Recap is active. You can get pretty granular. For example, you can have Siri Recap on only at the office during weekdays from 1PM to 4PM if that’s when you have meetings. This is hard to convey to bystanders, and I think ethical use should come with an in-person heads-up to the people you frequently interact with. (Hello, fellow Verge writers and editors.)
Live Rewind, so far, has worked as described — with the heavy caveat that I’ve only tested it in my quiet home office with my spouse. Even so, it takes a hot second to learn the timing of a double press. My spouse noticed the audible chime signaling the feature is in use, though they didn’t notice the animation. I’ll have to see how this fares in louder environments. Siri accurately captured our attempts to get my cat to roll over, though in subsequent tests, it misheard a word or two.
I’m more hesitant to comment on Siri Recap. It’s not just because I haven’t had many organic, lengthy spoken conversations yet since downloading the beta. (Siri did not deem my brief conversation with my spouse as worthy enough for recapping.) But I won’t really get a sense for how this feature feels until I’ve tested it in a wide variety of scenarios. Will it work if I talk to myself aloud? How well does it filter out gossip? How will this change how people speak to me? That’ll be the true test of this feature and Apple’s bystander privacy claims.
My first Siri Recap was for an editorial planning meeting for a story I’m working on. It was decent at identifying different topics discussed, and I was impressed that it stripped out some sensitive information. Any outsider looking at these notes would be terribly confused. Ironically, it meant that this summary wasn’t the most useful for my job.
What I will say is that I’ve been testing the Amazon Bee Frontier for the past few weeks. In the little time I’ve spent with the watchOS 27.3 beta, the differences between Audio Intelligence and the Bee are very clear. The latter has more of what I’d call an AI-forward presence. Bee, for example, offers insights about the emotional tone of a conversation. I’ve also found that the AI can be a bit judgy about insights and takeaways. Live Rewind is just a straight transcript. Apple’s said publicly that Siri Recap is meant to be highly factual notes to jog a person’s memory. That rings true based on my first one. And, as far as I can tell, there is no commerce angle for Siri Recaps, whereas Bee has an Amazon integration that surfaces buying suggestions based on conversations.
In any case, I’ll be diving deep into these features in the days to come. Let us know in the comments what you’re most curious about.

articles.title_orig: Elizabeth Warren will take over the Senate Banking Committee next year. Expect hearings.
articles.title_zh: Elizabeth Warren will take over the Senate Banking Committee next year. Expect hearings.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Democratic firebrand Elizabeth Warren, a consumer advocate known for her fierce battles over financial regulations, will take the gavel in January to become chair of the powerful Senate Banking Committee.
According to a source familiar with her plans, the Massachusetts senator intends to use her expanded platform to advance legislation to tackle populist affordability issues with a focus on housing.
The person familiar with her plans says Warren will use the committee's investigative powers to hold hearings and launch investigations into executive branch ethics and corporate practices, aiming to hold President Trump, the administration, Wall Street, and Big Tech accountable for economic decisions she views as having driven up costs for consumers.
Warren is also expected to take steps to shield the Federal Reserve from White House overreach . Any future nominee for the Fed will have to go through her committee. Earlier this year, she rallied Democrats to oppose Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's confirmation before the banking committee, stalling his eventual confirmation.
Wall Street is likely to be another of Warren's targets. Before Republicans regained control of Congress, Democrats would have the chief executives of big banks testify before the Senate Banking and House Financial Services committees once a year. The banking industry can expect a return to that practice.
Stephen Biggar, who covers the financial sector for Argus Research, says hearings will offer more transparency, but won't be accompanied by meaningful rulemaking. Biggar expects increased oversight, potentially more consumer protections, and actions to limit banks' market share size, such as blocking mergers.
He added that there are concerns that the deregulation efforts and lower capital requirements for banks championed by Republicans are now at risk.
James Angel, an associate professor at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, said he thinks the hearings will accomplish two things: producing information and sound bites that will get people to pay attention and galvanize public opinion. Second, Angel says they will serve as a deterrent for people in power.
"If people will be held under oath and there's a prospect of perjury, that will deter people from doing 'Trumpier' things," Angel said in an interview.
Angel also noted that any Trump appointee who has to be confirmed by Warren's committee will need to withstand bipartisan scrutiny and thus is more likely to be a moderate.
This summer, Warren teamed up with current Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott to pass a sprawling bipartisan housing bill that addresses housing affordability by encouraging more homebuilding, expanding financing options, and restricting large corporate investors buying single-family homes. Warren is expected to continue her push to rein in private equity across industries that she sees jacking up costs for families.
Warren also intends to conduct oversight into prediction markets and election betting platforms to prevent insider trading and platform manipulation. Before the midterm elections, Warren co-authored a letter with Utah Sen. John Curtis to executives of Kalshi and Polymarket asking them to explain how they would prevent candidates, campaign staff, and others with inside information from trading on election contracts.
There are also potential areas of common ground with Republicans, including advancing bipartisan AI export-control bills. Warren worked on three such bills this year, including a measure to stop advanced AI chips from being used by China to develop dangerous systems.
One area of agreement that could secure Trump's signature: capping credit card interest rates. It's something both Warren and Trump support, along with newly elected Democrats, including Texas's new senator, James Talarico.

articles.title_orig: Israel's Arab-led parties in spotlight after inconclusive election
articles.title_zh: Israel's Arab-led parties in spotlight after inconclusive election
articles.content_orig:
A Palestinian citizen of Israel casts her ballot in the country's general election at a polling station in Umm al-Fahm, Israel, Oct. 27, 2026 Mahmoud Illean/AP hide caption
KUFR QASI, Israel — In recent years many Palestinian citizens of Israel shunned elections, believing there was little to gain from participating in the politics of a state which, they say, regularly marginalizes their communities and oppresses their fellow Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
But last month, Palestinian Arabs in Israel came to the ballot boxes in record numbers, helping strip Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's most far-right government in Israel's history of its majority, and giving Arab-led parties the votes they needed to become a powerful force in Israeli politics.
"We blocked the government of Netanyahu from continuing," said Jamal Zahalka, chairman of the High Follow-Up Committee, the main umbrella body representing Palestinian citizens of Israel. "It's a historical achievement. I think our community found its strength."
Neither Netanyahu's coalition, nor his main challenger Gadi Eisenkot's center-right opposition, reached the threshold of 61 seats needed to form a government. Arab-led parties won 19 out of 120 seats — enough to give them a critical role in the negotiations that will now determine who governs Israel at this turbulent moment in the country's history.
The election results strike at the heart of the decades-long questions about how Israel defines itself and the role of Palestinian Arabs in its society.
At a park in the Palestinian-majority town of Kufr Qasim two days after the election, hundreds of people gathered for the annual commemoration of residents gunned down in 1956 by Israeli border police on the opening day of the Suez Crisis in the violent early years of the state, when Israel, Britain and France attacked Egypt after it nationalized the Suez Canal.
"And today we stand here, 70 years later," the speaker told the large crowd from a podium: "And the story still isn't over."
The crowd at this event, mostly dressed in black — some wearing the keffiyeh, the black and white stitched scarf symbolizing Palestinian resistance — mourned not only their lost relatives all those years ago, but also the suffering of Palestinians now: the sharp rise in discrimination against their communities in Israel since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023; Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and left a population to survive amid the ruins of the enclave. And the actions of Netanyahu's extreme right-wing government in the occupied West Bank, where rights groups and the U.N. say it has armed and supported settlers as they force Palestinians from their homes and agricultural lands with unprecedented violence.
Worsening rights inside Israel was one reason, residents of Kufr Qasm told NPR, why so many Palestinian citizens in Israel went to the ballot boxes. "There is no freedom anymore," said Intisar Sarsur, 65, sitting with relatives beside an olive tree in the park in Kufr Qasim. " We are seeking for our basic rights as human beings."
"Everybody that I know participated in the elections. Not one person stayed home," Sarsur said. She and her family were sharing platters of mutabbaq , a sweet Palestinian layered pastry, and freshly pressed olive oil from this year's olive harvest — usually a joyous moment in the Palestinian calendar, that she said now felt bittersweet. This year the olive harvest for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank was marred by frequent attacks by Israeli settlers trying to disrupt this economically and culturally significant time of year.
Mansour Abbas, a lawmaker in Israel's parliament and leader of the conservative Muslim Ra'am party, embraces a supporter after the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election in Sakhnin, Israel, on Oct. 27. Mahmoud Illean/AP hide caption
Palestinian citizens of Israel, descendants of those who remained as the state of Israel was established in 1948 (when a majority of the prewar population was forcibly expelled or fled during the war) now make up about 20% of the population.
This election, Arab-led parties received a 64% increase in votes compared to the last elections, according to the Central Elections Committee. The gains they made have stirred anger, and even fear, among many on Israel's political right, who see them as a threat to the country's Jewish character.
Netanyahu and his allies made the large Arab turnout a rallying cry. On election day, Netanyahu posted a video calling it an "emergency." Itamar Ben Gvir, the far-right national security minister, filmed his own appeal at the entrance to Kufr Qasim: "If you want this country to remain Jewish and Zionist … then get out and vote!"
As results came in, Netanyahu's Likud party went further. It claimed Arab parties had "stolen" the election through bribery, threats and forgery, and later warned of a foreign takeover of the Knesset and the "Islamization of Israel." The party has made no evidence public. Police say they found no basis for the claims, and election officials say there was no widespread fraud. The head of the elections committee separately asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate suspected foreign funding of efforts to boost Arab turnout. But he and the attorney general say the vote was conducted properly and the results were not compromised.
The messaging by Netanyahu's bloc is widely seen as an attempt to prevent Eisenkot's center-right grouping from partnering with Arab parties — a reality that would give Eisenkot the majority he needs to form a government. But the sharp rise in anti-Arab sentiment since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks, in which some 1,200 people were killed, has made an alliance with any Arab party potentially politically treacherous and could cause other Jewish right wing members of his bloc to split off in fury.
Eisenkot is not a natural ally for Arab parties either. A former military chief of staff whose son was killed fighting in Gaza, he served as an observer in Netanyahu's war cabinet early in the war. And he still cuts a hawkish figure. As a general, he is credited with formulating the "Dahiyeh doctrine," which he laid out in 2008: using "disproportionate force" against villages from which militants fire on Israel, which he called "not civilian villages" but "military bases." It is named after Beirut's southern suburbs, a Hezbollah stronghold that Israel largely decimated in heavy bombardment in 2006.
Campaign billboards show the Ra'am party (left) and the Joint List of Arab-led parties in the Bedouin city of Rahat, southern Israel, Nov. 1. David Goldman/AP hide caption
So Arab parties are divided on how to use the power they gained in this election. Ra'am, a socially conservative Islamist party, campaigned on joining a governing coalition and put a Jewish former police official second on its list. But for now the Joint List alliance that won 11 of the 19 Arab-led party seats in this election won't formally partner with Eisenkot. Its leaders have said they could back his government from the outside, but won't join it, citing Israel's ongoing war in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.
President Isaac Herzog has been consulting with parties over who they would support to try to form a coalition. He is expected to announce which candidate he'll give a mandate to next week, to try to form a coalition. That candidate will have 28 days and can ask for a further two-week extension. If he fails, another candidate is given only 28 days (without extension) to try to form a government. And if no one manages to form a coalition, there will be repeat elections next year.
In Kufr Qasim, as the readings and re-enactments of the 1956 killings unfurled on stage, Mansour Shaaban said he would vote again in an instant. Aged 33, this was the first election he had voted in. But now he said it's necessary to try to stop what he ca
